economists such as <color=#3366CC>Robert Lucas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thomas Sargent</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Edward Prescott</color>. They introduced the notion of rational
expectations in economics, which had profound implications for many economic discussions, including the so-called
Lucas critique and the development of real business cycle models.
New Keynesians
During the 1980s, a group of researchers came to be known as New Keynesian economists, including, among others,
<color=#3366CC>George Akerlof</color>, <color=#3366CC>Janet Yellen</color>, Gregory Mankiw, and <color=#3366CC>Olivier Blanchard</color>. They adopted the principle of rational
expectations and other monetarist or new classical ideas, such as models employing microfoundations and optimizing
behaviour, but simultaneously emphasized the importance of various <color=#3366CC>market failures</color> in the functioning of the economy,
as had Keynes. Not least, they proposed various reasons that potentially explained the empirically observed features of
price and wage rigidity, usually made to be endogenous features of the models, rather than assumed as in older
Keynesian-style ones.
New neoclassical synthesis
After decades of often heated discussions among Keynesians, monetarists, new classical and new Keynesian
economists, a synthesis emerged by the 2000s, often called the new neoclassical synthesis. It integrated the
rational-expectations and optimizing framework of the new classical theory with a new-Keynesian role for nominal
rigidities and other market imperfections, such as <color=#3366CC>imperfect information</color>, in goods, labour, and credit markets. The
monetarist importance of monetary policy in stabilizing the economy and in particular controlling inflation was
recognised as well as the traditional Keynesian insistence that fiscal policy could also play an influential role in affecting
aggregate demand. Methodologically, the synthesis led to a new class of applied models, known as dynamic stochastic
general equilibrium (DSGE) models, derived from real business cycle models but extended with several new-Keynesian
and other features. These models proved useful and influential in the design of modern monetary policy and are now
standard workhorses in most central banks.
After the 2008 financial crisis
After the <color=#3366CC>2008 financial crisis</color>, macroeconomic research has placed greater emphasis on understanding and integrating
the financial system into models of the broader economy, and on shedding light on how problems in the financial sector
can trigger major macroeconomic recessions. In this and other branches of research, inspiration from <color=#3366CC>behavioural</color>
<color=#3366CC>economics</color> has begun to play a more important role in mainstream economic theory. Also, heterogeneity among the
economic agents, e.g., differences in income, plays an increasing role in recent economic research.
Other schools and approaches
Other schools or trends of thought referring to a particular style of economics practised at and disseminated from
well-defined groups of academicians that have become known worldwide, include the Freiburg School, the School of
Lausanne, the Stockholm school and the <color=#3366CC>Chicago school of economics</color>. During the 1970s and 1980s mainstream
economics was sometimes separated into the Saltwater approach of those universities along the Eastern and Western
coasts of the US, and the Freshwater, or <color=#3366CC>Chicago school</color> approach.
Within macroeconomics there is, in general order of their historical appearance in the literature; <color=#3366CC>classical economics</color>,
<color=#3366CC>neoclassical economics</color>, <color=#3366CC>Keynesian economics</color>, the neoclassical synthesis, <color=#3366CC>monetarism</color>, new classical economics, New
Keynesian economics and the new neoclassical synthesis.
Besides the mainstream development of economic thought, various alternative or heterodox economic theories have
evolved, positioning themselves in contrast to mainstream theory. These include:
• <color=#3366CC>Austrian School</color>, emphasising human action, <color=#3366CC>property rights</color>, and the freedom to contract and transact to have a
thriving and successful economy. It also emphasises that the state should play as small a role as possible (if any
role) in the regulation of economic activity between two transacting parties. <color=#3366CC>Friedrich Hayek</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ludwig von Mises</color>
are the two most prominent representatives of the Austrian school.
• Post-Keynesian economics concentrates on macroeconomic rigidities and adjustment processes. It is generally
associated with the <color=#3366CC>University of Cambridge</color> and the work of <color=#3366CC>Joan Robinson</color>.
• Ecological economics like environmental economics studies the interactions between human economies and the
ecosystems in which they are embedded, but in contrast to environmental economics takes an oppositional
position towards general mainstream economic principles. A major difference between the two subdisciplines is
their assumptions about the substitution possibilities between human-made and natural capital.
Additionally, alternative developments include Marxian economics, constitutional economics, institutional economics,
evolutionary economics, dependency theory, structuralist economics, <color=#3366CC>world systems theory</color>, econophysics,
econodynamics, feminist economics and biophysical economics.
Feminist economics emphasises the role of gender in economies, challenging analyses that render gender invisible or
that support gender-oppressive economic systems. The goal is to create economic research and policy analysis that is
inclusive and gender-aware to encourage gender equality and improve the well-being of marginalised groups.
Methodology
Theoretical research
Mainstream economic theory relies upon analytical <color=#3366CC>economic models</color>. When creating theories, the objective is to find
assumptions that are at least as simple in information requirements, more precise in predictions, and more fruitful in
generating additional research than prior theories. While <color=#3366CC>neoclassical</color> economic theory constitutes both the dominant or
orthodox theoretical as well as methodological framework, economic theory can also take the form of other schools of
thought such as in heterodox economic theories.

In <color=#3366CC>microeconomics</color>, principal concepts include <color=#3366CC>supply and demand</color>, marginalism, <color=#3366CC>rational choice theory</color>, <color=#3366CC>opportunity</color>
<color=#3366CC>cost</color>, budget constraints, <color=#3366CC>utility</color>, and the theory of the firm. Early <color=#3366CC>macroeconomic</color> models focused on modelling the
relationships between aggregate variables, but as the relationships appeared to change over time, macroeconomists,
including new Keynesians, reformulated their models with microfoundations, in which microeconomic concepts play a
major part.
Sometimes an economic hypothesis is only qualitative, not quantitative.
Expositions of economic reasoning often use two-dimensional graphs to illustrate theoretical relationships. At a higher
level of generality, mathematical economics is the application of <color=#3366CC>mathematical</color> methods to represent theories and
analyse problems in economics. <color=#3366CC>Paul Samuelson</color>'s treatise Foundations of Economic Analysis (1947) exemplifies the
method, particularly in its treatment of maximizing behavioural relations among agents as they reach equilibrium. The
book focused on examining the class of statements called operationally meaningful theorems in economics, which are
<color=#3366CC>theorems</color> that can conceivably be refuted by empirical data.
Empirical research
Economic theories are frequently tested empirically, largely through the use of <color=#3366CC>econometrics</color> using economic data. The
controlled experiments common to the physical sciences are difficult and uncommon in economics, and instead broad
data is <color=#3366CC>observationally studied</color>; this type of testing is typically regarded as less rigorous than controlled
experimentation, and the conclusions typically more tentative. However, the field of experimental economics is growing,
and the use of natural experiments is increasing.
<color=#3366CC>Statistical methods</color> such as <color=#3366CC>regression analysis</color> are common. Practitioners use such methods to estimate the size,
economic significance, and <color=#3366CC>statistical significance</color> ("signal strength") of the hypothesised relation(s) and to adjust for
noise from other variables. By such means, a hypothesis may gain acceptance, although in a probabilistic, rather than
certain, sense. Acceptance is dependent upon the <color=#3366CC>falsifiable</color> hypothesis surviving tests. The use of commonly accepted
methods need not produce a conclusion or even a consensus on a particular question, given different tests, data sets,
and prior beliefs.
Experimental economics has promoted the use of scientifically controlled <color=#3366CC>experiments</color>. This has reduced the long-noted
distinction between economics and the <color=#3366CC>natural sciences</color> because it allows direct tests of what were previously taken as
axioms. In some cases these have found that the axioms are not entirely correct.
In <color=#3366CC>behavioural economics</color>, psychologist <color=#3366CC>Daniel Kahneman</color> won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2002 for his and Amos
Tversky's empirical discovery of several <color=#3366CC>cognitive biases</color> and heuristics. Similar empirical testing occurs in
neuroeconomics. Another example is the assumption of narrowly selfish preferences versus a model that tests for
selfish, altruistic, and cooperative preferences. These techniques have led some to argue that economics is a "genuine
science".
Microeconomics
Microeconomics examines how entities, forming a <color=#3366CC>market structure</color>, interact within a <color=#3366CC>market</color> to create a market system.
These entities include private and public players with various classifications, typically operating under scarcity of
tradable units and <color=#3366CC>regulation</color>. The item traded may be a tangible <color=#3366CC>product</color>, such as apples, or a <color=#3366CC>service</color>, such as repair
services, legal counsel, or entertainment.
Various market structures exist. In <color=#3366CC>perfectly competitive markets</color>, no participant is large enough to have the market
power to set the price of a homogeneous product. In other words, every participant is a "price taker" because no single
participant can influence the product's price. In the real world, markets often experience imperfect competition.
Forms of imperfect competition include <color=#3366CC>monopoly</color> (in which there is only one seller of a good), duopoly (in which there
are only two sellers of a good), oligopoly (in which there are few sellers of a good), monopolistic competition (in which
many sellers are producing highly differentiated goods), monopsony (in which there is only one buyer of a good), and
oligopsony (in which there are few buyers of a good). Firms under imperfect competition have the potential to be "price
makers", meaning they can influence the prices of their products.
In the partial equilibrium method of analysis, it is assumed that activity in the market being analysed does not affect
other markets. This method aggregates (the sum of all activity) in only one market. General-equilibrium theory studies
various markets and their behaviour. It aggregates (the sum of all activity) across all markets. This method studies both
changes in markets and their interactions that lead to equilibrium.
Production, cost, and efficiency
In microeconomics, <color=#3366CC>production</color> is the conversion of <color=#3366CC>inputs</color> into <color=#3366CC>outputs</color>. It is an economic process that uses inputs to
create a <color=#3366CC>commodity</color> or a service for <color=#3366CC>exchange</color> or direct use. Production is a flow, and thus a rate of output per period.
Distinctions include such production alternatives as for <color=#3366CC>consumption</color> (food, haircuts, etc.) vs. <color=#3366CC>investment goods</color> (new
tractors, buildings, roads, etc.), <color=#3366CC>public goods</color> (national defence, smallpox vaccinations, etc.) or <color=#3366CC>private goods</color>, and
"guns" vs "butter".
Inputs used in the production process include such primary <color=#3366CC>factors of production</color> as <color=#3366CC>labour services</color>, <color=#3366CC>capital</color> (durable
produced goods used in production, such as an existing factory), and land (including natural resources). Other inputs
may include intermediate goods used in the production of final goods, such as the steel in a new car.
Economic efficiency measures how well a system generates desired output with a given set of inputs and available
<color=#3366CC>technology</color>. Efficiency improves when more output is generated without changing inputs. A widely accepted general
standard is <color=#3366CC>Pareto efficiency</color>, which is reached when no further change can make someone better off without making
someone else worse off.
The <color=#3366CC>production–possibility frontier</color> (PPF) is a graphical representation of scarcity, opportunity cost, and efficiency. In the
simplest case, an <color=#3366CC>economy</color> can produce just two goods (say "guns" and "butter"). The PPF is a table or graph (as
shown on the right) that shows the different combinations of quantities of the two goods that can be produced with a
given technology and total factor inputs, which limit feasible total output. Each point on the curve shows potential total
output for the economy, which is the maximum feasible output of one good, given a feasible output quantity of the other
good.
<color=#3366CC>Scarcity</color> is represented in the figure by people being willing but unable in the aggregate to consume beyond the PPF
(such as at X) and by the negative slope of the curve. If production of one good increases along the curve, production
of the other good decreases, an inverse relationship. This is because increasing the output of one good requires
reallocating inputs from the production of the other good, thereby decreasing the latter.
The slope of the curve at a point on it gives the trade-off between the two goods. It measures what an additional unit of
one good costs in terms of the units of the other good forgone, an example of a real opportunity cost. Thus, if one more
Gun costs 100 units of butter, the opportunity cost of one Gun is 100 units of butter. Along the PPF, scarcity implies
that choosing more of one good in the aggregate entails doing with less of the other good. Still, in a <color=#3366CC>market economy</color>,
movement along the curve may indicate that the <color=#3366CC>choice</color> of the increased output is anticipated to be worth the cost to the
agents.
By construction, each point on the curve represents productive efficiency in maximizing output for a given set of total
inputs. A point inside the curve (as at A) is feasible but represents production inefficiency (wasteful use of inputs), in
that output of one or both goods could increase by moving in a northeast direction to a point on the curve. Examples
cited of such inefficiency include high <color=#3366CC>unemployment</color> during a <color=#3366CC>business-cycle</color> <color=#3366CC>recession</color> or an economic organisation of
a country that discourages the full use of resources. Being on the curve might still not fully satisfy <color=#3366CC>allocative efficiency</color>
(also called <color=#3366CC>Pareto efficiency</color>) if it does not produce a mix of goods that consumers prefer over other points.
Much applied economics in <color=#3366CC>public policy</color> is concerned with determining how the efficiency of an economy can be
improved. Recognizing the reality of scarcity and then figuring out how to organise society for the most efficient use of
resources has been described as the "essence of economics", in which the subject "makes its unique contribution."
Specialisation
Specialisation is considered key to economic efficiency based on theoretical and empirical considerations. Different
individuals or nations may have different real opportunity costs of production, for example, due to differences in stocks
of human capital per worker or <color=#3366CC>capital</color>-to-labour ratios. According to theory, this may give a <color=#3366CC>comparative advantage</color> in
the production of goods that make more intensive use of the relatively more abundant, thus relatively cheaper, input.
Even if one region has an absolute advantage as to the ratio of its outputs to inputs in every type of output, it may still
specialise in the output in which it has a comparative advantage and thereby gain from trading with a region that lacks
any absolute advantage but has a comparative advantage in producing something else.
It has been observed that a high volume of trade occurs among regions, even when they have access to similar
technology and a similar mix of factor inputs, including high-income countries. This has led to the investigation of
economies of scale and agglomeration to explain specialisation in similar yet differentiated product lines, benefiting the
respective trading partners or regions.
The general theory of specialisation applies to trade among individuals, farms, manufacturers, <color=#3366CC>service</color> providers, and
<color=#3366CC>economies</color>. Among these production systems, there may be a corresponding <color=#3366CC>division of labour</color> with different work
groups specializing, or correspondingly different types of <color=#3366CC>capital equipment</color> and differentiated land uses.
An example that combines the features above is a country that specialises in producing high-tech knowledge products,
as developed countries do, and trades with developing nations for goods produced in factories where labour is
relatively cheap and plentiful, resulting in different opportunity costs of production. More total output and utility result
from specializing in production and trade than from each country producing its own high-tech and low-tech products.
Theory and observation set out the conditions such that market <color=#3366CC>prices</color> of outputs and productive inputs select an
allocation of factor inputs by comparative advantage, so that (relatively) <color=#3366CC>low-cost</color> inputs go to producing low-cost
outputs. In the process, aggregate output may increase as a <color=#3366CC>by-product</color> or by design. Such specialisation of production
creates opportunities for gains from trade whereby resource owners benefit from <color=#3366CC>trade</color> in the sale of one type of output
for other, more highly valued goods. A measure of gains from trade is the increased income levels that trade may
facilitate.
Supply and demand
Prices and quantities have been described as the most directly observable attributes of goods produced and
exchanged in a <color=#3366CC>market economy</color>. The theory of supply and demand is an organizing principle for explaining how prices
coordinate the amounts produced and consumed. In <color=#3366CC>microeconomics</color>, it applies to price and output determination for a
market with <color=#3366CC>perfect competition</color>, which includes the condition of no buyers or sellers large enough to have price-setting
power.
For a given market of a <color=#3366CC>commodity</color>, demand is the relation of the quantity that all buyers would be prepared to
purchase at each unit price of the good. Demand is often represented by a table or a graph showing the relationship
between price and quantity demanded (as in the figure). Demand theory describes individual consumers as <color=#3366CC>rationally</color>
choosing the most preferred quantity of each good, given income, prices, tastes, etc. A term for this is "constrained
utility maximisation" (with income and <color=#3366CC>wealth</color> as the constraints on demand). Here, <color=#3366CC>utility</color> refers to the hypothesised
relation of each consumer for ranking different commodity bundles as more or less preferred.
The <color=#3366CC>law of demand</color> states that, in general, price and quantity demanded in a given market are inversely related. That is,
the higher the price of a product, the less of it people would be prepared to buy (other things unchanged). As the price
of a commodity falls, consumers move toward it from relatively more expensive goods (the substitution effect). In
addition, the price decline increases purchasing power, thereby increasing the ability to buy (the income effect). Other
factors can change demand; for example, an increase in income will shift the demand curve for a normal good outward,
as shown in the figure. All determinants are treated as constant factors in demand and supply.
Supply is the relation between the price of a good and the quantity available for sale at that price. It may be
represented as a table or graph relating price and quantity supplied. Producers, for example, business firms, are
hypothesized to be profit maximizers, meaning they attempt to produce and supply the quantity of goods that yields the
highest profit. Supply is typically represented as a function relating price and quantity, if other factors are unchanged.
That is, the higher the price at which the good can be sold, the more of it producers will supply, as in the figure. The
higher price makes it profitable to increase production. Just as on the demand side, the position of the supply curve can
shift, say, due to a change in the price of a productive input or a technical improvement. The "Law of Supply" states
that, in general, a rise in price leads to an expansion in supply and a fall in price leads to a contraction in supply. Here
as well, the determinants of supply, such as the prices of substitutes, the cost of production, the technology used, and
other factors of production, are assumed constant over the specific time period under evaluation.
<color=#3366CC>Market equilibrium</color> occurs where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, the intersection of the supply and
demand curves in the figure above. At a price below the equilibrium, there is a shortage of quantity supplied compared
to quantity demanded. This is posited to bid up the price. At a price above equilibrium, there is a surplus of quantity
supplied compared to quantity demanded. This pushes the price down. The <color=#3366CC>model</color> of supply and demand predicts that
for given supply and demand curves, price and quantity will stabilise at the price that makes quantity supplied equal to
quantity demanded. Similarly, demand-and-supply theory predicts a new price-quantity combination from a shift in
demand (as shown in the figure) or in supply.
Firms
People frequently do not trade directly on markets. Instead, on the supply side, they may work in and produce through

firms. The most obvious kinds of firms are <color=#3366CC>corporations</color>, <color=#3366CC>partnerships</color> and <color=#3366CC>trusts</color>. According to <color=#3366CC>Ronald Coase</color>, people
begin to organise their production within firms when the costs of doing business become lower than those of doing it on
the market. Firms combine labour and capital, and can achieve far greater <color=#3366CC>economies of scale</color> (when the average cost
per unit declines as more units are produced) than individual market trading.
In <color=#3366CC>perfectly competitive</color> markets studied in the theory of supply and demand, there are many producers, none of which
significantly influence price. Industrial organisation generalises from that special case to study the strategic behaviour
of firms that have significant control of price. It considers the structure of such markets and their interactions. Common
market structures studied besides perfect competition include monopolistic competition, various forms of oligopoly, and
monopoly.
Managerial economics applies <color=#3366CC>microeconomic</color> analysis to specific decisions in business firms or other management
units. It draws heavily on quantitative methods, such as <color=#3366CC>operations research</color> and programming, and on statistical
methods, such as <color=#3366CC>regression analysis</color>, in the absence of certainty and perfect knowledge. A unifying theme is the
attempt to <color=#3366CC>optimise</color> business decisions, including unit-cost minimisation and profit maximisation, given the firm's
objectives and the constraints imposed by technology and market conditions.
Uncertainty and game theory
<color=#3366CC>Uncertainty</color> in economics is an unknown prospect of gain or loss, whether quantifiable as <color=#3366CC>risk</color> or not. Without it,
household behaviour would be unaffected by uncertain employment and income prospects, <color=#3366CC>financial</color> and <color=#3366CC>capital</color>
<color=#3366CC>markets</color> would reduce to the exchange of a single instrument in each market period, and there would be no
<color=#3366CC>communications</color> industry. Given its different forms, there are various ways of representing uncertainty and modelling
economic agents' responses to it.
<color=#3366CC>Game theory</color> is a branch of <color=#3366CC>applied mathematics</color> that considers <color=#3366CC>strategic interactions</color> between agents, one kind of
uncertainty. It provides a mathematical foundation of industrial organisation, discussed above, to model different types
of firm behaviour, for example in a solipsistic industry (few sellers), but equally applicable to wage negotiations,
bargaining, contract design, and any situation where individual agents are few enough to have perceptible effects on
each other. In <color=#3366CC>behavioural economics</color>, it has been used to model the strategies agents choose when interacting with
others whose interests are at least partially adverse to their own.
In this, it generalises maximisation approaches developed to analyse market actors, such as the <color=#3366CC>supply and demand</color>
model, and allows for incomplete information among actors. The field dates from the 1944 classic Theory of Games
and Economic Behavior by <color=#3366CC>John von Neumann</color> and Oskar Morgenstern. It has significant applications seemingly
outside of economics in such diverse subjects as the formulation of nuclear strategies, <color=#3366CC>ethics</color>, <color=#3366CC>political science</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>evolutionary biology</color>.
Risk aversion may stimulate activity that, in well-functioning markets, smooths out risk and communicates information
about it, as in markets for <color=#3366CC>insurance</color>, commodity <color=#3366CC>futures contracts</color>, and financial instruments. Financial economics or
simply <color=#3366CC>finance</color> describes the allocation of financial resources. It also analyses the pricing of financial instruments, the
financial structure of companies, the efficiency and fragility of <color=#3366CC>financial markets</color>, <color=#3366CC>financial crises</color>, and related
government policy or <color=#3366CC>regulation</color>.
Some market organisations may give rise to inefficiencies due to uncertainty. Based on <color=#3366CC>George Akerlof</color>'s "Market for
Lemons" article, the <color=#3366CC>paradigm</color> example is of a dodgy second-hand car market. Customers who do not know whether a
car is a "lemon" depress its price below that of a quality second-hand car. Information asymmetry arises here, if the
seller has more relevant information than the buyer but no incentive to disclose it. Related problems in insurance are
adverse selection, such that those at most risk are most likely to insure (say reckless drivers), and moral hazard, such
that insurance results in riskier behaviour (say more reckless driving).
Both problems may raise insurance costs and reduce efficiency by driving otherwise willing transactors from the market
("incomplete markets"). Moreover, attempting to reduce one problem, say adverse selection by mandating insurance,
may add to another, say moral hazard. Information economics, which studies such problems, is relevant to subjects
such as insurance, contract law, mechanism design, monetary economics, and health care. Applied subjects include
market and legal remedies to spread or reduce risk, such as warranties, government-mandated partial insurance,
restructuring or <color=#3366CC>bankruptcy law</color>, inspection, and regulation for quality and information disclosure.
Market failure
The term "<color=#3366CC>market failure</color>" encompasses several problems that may undermine standard economic assumptions.
Although economists categorise market failures differently, the following categories emerge in the main texts.
Information asymmetries and incomplete markets may result in economic inefficiency, but also present opportunities to
improve efficiency through market, legal, and regulatory remedies, as discussed above.
Natural monopoly, or the overlapping concepts of "practical" and "technical" monopoly, is an extreme case of failure of
competition as a restraint on producers. Extreme <color=#3366CC>economies of scale</color> are one possible cause.
<color=#3366CC>Public goods</color> are goods that are under-supplied in a typical market. The defining features are that people can consume
public goods without paying for them and that more than one person can consume the good at the same time.
<color=#3366CC>Externalities</color> occur where there are high social costs or benefits from production or consumption that are not reflected
in market prices. For example, air pollution may generate a negative externality, and education may generate a positive
externality (e.g., lower crime). Governments often tax and otherwise restrict the sale of goods that have negative
externalities and subsidise or otherwise promote the purchase of goods that have positive externalities in an effort to
correct the price distortions caused by these externalities. Elementary demand-and-supply theory predicts equilibrium
but not the speed of adjustment for changes of equilibrium due to a shift in demand or supply.
In many areas, some form of price stickiness is postulated to account for quantities, rather than prices, adjusting in the
short run to changes in demand or supply. This includes standard analysis of the <color=#3366CC>business cycle</color> in <color=#3366CC>macroeconomics</color>.
Analysis often revolves around causes of such price stickiness and their implications for reaching a hypothesised
long-run equilibrium. Examples of such price stickiness in particular markets include wage rates in labour markets and
posted prices in markets deviate from <color=#3366CC>perfect competition</color>.
Some specialised fields of economics deal with market failure more than others. The economics of the public sector is
one example. Much environmental economics concerns externalities or "public bads".
<color=#3366CC>Policy</color> options include regulations that reflect <color=#3366CC>cost–benefit analysis</color> or market solutions that change incentives, such as
emission fees or redefinition of property rights.
Welfare
Welfare economics uses microeconomics techniques to evaluate <color=#3366CC>well-being</color> from allocation of <color=#3366CC>productive factors</color> as to
desirability and economic efficiency within an <color=#3366CC>economy</color>, often relative to competitive general equilibrium. It analyses
social welfare, however measured, in terms of economic activities of the individuals that compose the theoretical
society considered. Accordingly, individuals, with associated economic activities, are the basic units for aggregating to
social welfare, whether of a group, a community, or a society, and there is no "social welfare" apart from the "welfare"
associated with its individual units.
Macroeconomics
Macroeconomics, another branch of economics, examines the economy as a whole to explain broad aggregates and
their interactions "top down", that is, using a simplified form of general-equilibrium theory. Such aggregates include
national income and output, the <color=#3366CC>unemployment rate</color>, and price <color=#3366CC>inflation</color> and subaggregates like total consumption and
investment spending and their components. It also studies the effects of <color=#3366CC>monetary policy</color> and <color=#3366CC>fiscal policy</color>.
Since at least the 1960s, macroeconomics has been characterised by further integration as to micro-based modelling of
sectors, including rationality of players, efficient use of market information, and imperfect competition. This has
addressed a long-standing concern about inconsistent developments of the same subject.
Macroeconomic analysis also considers factors affecting the long-term level and <color=#3366CC>growth</color> of national income. Such
factors include capital accumulation, technological change, and labour force growth.
Growth
Growth economics studies factors that explain <color=#3366CC>economic growth</color> – the increase in output per capita of a country over a
long period of time. The same factors are used to explain differences in the level of output per capita between
countries, in particular why some countries grow faster than others, and whether countries converge at the same rates
of growth.
Much-studied factors include the rate of investment, <color=#3366CC>population growth</color>, and technological change. These are
represented in theoretical and empirical forms (as in the neoclassical and endogenous growth models) and in growth
accounting.
Business cycle
The economics of a depression spurred the creation of "macroeconomics" as a separate discipline. During the <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Depression</color> of the 1930s, <color=#3366CC>John Maynard Keynes</color> authored a book entitled <color=#3366CC>The General Theory of Employment, Interest</color>
<color=#3366CC>and Money</color>, outlining the key theories of <color=#3366CC>Keynesian economics</color>. Keynes contended that aggregate demand for goods
might be insufficient during economic downturns, leading to unnecessarily high unemployment and losses of potential
output.
He therefore advocated active policy responses by the public sector, including <color=#3366CC>monetary policy</color> actions by the <color=#3366CC>central</color>
<color=#3366CC>bank</color> and <color=#3366CC>fiscal policy</color> actions by the government, to stabilize output over the <color=#3366CC>business cycle</color>. Thus, a central conclusion
of Keynesian economics is that, in some situations, no strong automatic mechanism moves output and employment
towards <color=#3366CC>full employment</color> levels. <color=#3366CC>John Hicks</color>' IS/LM model has been the most influential interpretation of The General
Theory.
Over the years, the understanding of the <color=#3366CC>business cycle</color> has branched into various research programs, mostly related
to or distinct from Keynesianism. The neoclassical synthesis refers to the reconciliation of Keynesian economics with
<color=#3366CC>classical economics</color>, stating that Keynesianism is correct in the short run but qualified by classical-like considerations in
the intermediate and long run.
New classical macroeconomics, as distinct from the Keynesian view of the business cycle, posits market clearing with
<color=#3366CC>imperfect information</color>. It includes Friedman's permanent income hypothesis on consumption and "rational expectations"
theory, led by <color=#3366CC>Robert Lucas</color>, and real business cycle theory.
In contrast, the new Keynesian approach retains the rational expectations assumption; however, it assumes a variety of
<color=#3366CC>market failures</color>. In particular, New Keynesians assume that prices and wages are "sticky", meaning they do not adjust
instantaneously to changes in economic conditions.
Thus, the new classical economists assume that prices and wages adjust automatically to attain full employment. In
contrast, the new Keynesians see full employment as being automatically achieved only in the long run. Hence,
government and central-bank policies are needed because the "long run" may be very long.
Unemployment
The unemployment rate measures the level of unemployment in an economy, the percentage of workers in the labour
force who are unemployed. The labour force includes only workers actively looking for jobs. People who are retired,
pursuing education, or discouraged from seeking work by a lack of job prospects are excluded from the labour force.
Unemployment can generally be broken down into several types, each related to different causes.
Classical models of unemployment arise when wages are too high for employers to hire more workers. Consistent with
classical unemployment, frictional unemployment occurs when appropriate job vacancies exist for a worker, but the
time required to search for and find a job results in a period of unemployment.
Structural unemployment encompasses a variety of causes, including a mismatch between workers' skills and the skills
required for available jobs. Large amounts of structural unemployment can occur when an economy is transitioning
industries and workers find their previous set of skills are no longer in demand. Structural unemployment is similar to
frictional unemployment since both reflect the problem of matching workers with job vacancies, but structural
unemployment covers the time needed to acquire new skills, not just the short-term search process.
While some types of unemployment may occur regardless of the condition of the economy, cyclical unemployment
occurs when growth stagnates. Okun's law represents the empirical relationship between unemployment and economic
growth. The original version of Okun's law states that a 3% increase in output would lead to a 1% decrease in
unemployment.
Money and monetary policy
<color=#3366CC>Money</color> is a means of final payment for goods in most price system economies, and is the <color=#3366CC>unit of account</color> in which
prices are typically stated. Money has general acceptability, relative consistency in value, divisibility, durability,
portability, elasticity in supply, and longevity with mass public confidence. It includes currency held by the nonbank
public and checkable deposits. It has been described as a <color=#3366CC>social convention</color>, like language, useful to one largely
because it is useful to others. In the words of Francis Amasa Walker, a well-known 19th-century economist, "Money is
what money does" ("Money is that money does" in the original).
As a medium of exchange, money facilitates trade. It is essentially a measure of value and, more importantly, a store of
value, being a basis for credit creation. Its economic function can be contrasted with <color=#3366CC>barter</color> (non-monetary exchange).
Given a diverse array of produced goods and specialised producers, barter may entail a hard-to-locate double
coincidence of wants as to what is exchanged, say apples and a book. Money can reduce the transaction cost of
exchange because of its ready acceptability. Then it is less costly for the seller to accept money in exchange than to
accept what the buyer produces.
Monetary policy is the set of actions central banks take to achieve their broader objectives. Most central banks in
developed countries follow inflation targeting, whereas the main objective for many central banks in development
countries is to uphold a fixed exchange rate system. Central banks conduct monetary policy by setting a target for its
policy rate. Central banks implement policy by using monetary policy tools to steer the policy rate to the target.The
primary monetary tool is normally the adjustment of administered interest rates, or via open market operations. Via the
monetary transmission mechanism, interest rate changes affect <color=#3366CC>investment</color>, <color=#3366CC>consumption</color> and <color=#3366CC>net export</color>, and hence
aggregate demand, <color=#3366CC>output</color> and employment, and ultimately the development of wages and inflation.
Fiscal policy
Governments implement fiscal policy to influence macroeconomic conditions by adjusting spending and taxation
policies to alter aggregate demand. When aggregate demand falls below the economy's potential output, there is an
output gap in which some productive capacity remains idle. Governments increase spending and cut taxes to boost
aggregate demand. The government can use idled resources.
For example, unemployed home builders can be hired to expand highways. Tax cuts allow consumers to increase their
spending, which boosts aggregate demand. Both tax cuts and spending have multiplier effects, in which the initial
increase in demand from the policy percolates through the economy, generating additional economic activity.
The effects of fiscal policy can be limited by crowding out. When there is no output gap, the economy is producing at
full capacity, with no excess productive resources. If the government increases spending in this situation, it diverts
resources that the private sector would otherwise use, so overall output does not increase. Some economists think that
crowding out is always an issue, while others do not think it is a major issue when output is depressed.
Sceptics of fiscal policy also make the argument based on Ricardian equivalence. They argue that an increase in debt
will have to be paid for with future tax increases, which will cause people to reduce their consumption and save money
to pay for those increases. Under Ricardian equivalence, any boost in demand from tax cuts will be offset by the
increased savings intended to pay for future higher taxes.
Inequality
Economic inequality includes income inequality, measured using the distribution of income (the amount of money
people receive), and wealth inequality measured using the distribution of wealth (the amount of wealth people own),
and other measures such as consumption, land ownership, and human capital. Inequality exists to varying degrees
among countries or states, groups of people, and individuals. There are many methods for measuring inequality, the
<color=#3366CC>Gini coefficient</color> being widely used for income differences among individuals. An example measure of inequality
between countries is the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index, a composite index that accounts for
inequality. Important concepts of equality include equity, equality of outcome, and equality of opportunity.
Research has linked economic inequality to political and social instability, including <color=#3366CC>revolution</color>, democratic breakdown,
and civil conflict. Research suggests that greater inequality hinders economic growth and macroeconomic stability, and
that land and human capital inequality reduce growth more than inequality of income. Inequality is at the centre stage of
<color=#3366CC>economic policy</color> debate across the globe, as government tax and spending policies have significant effects on income
distribution. In advanced economies, taxes and transfers decrease income inequality by one-third, with most of this
being achieved via public social spending (such as pensions and family benefits).
Other branches of economics
Public economics
Public economics is the branch of economics that studies the economic activities of the public sector, usually the
government. The subject addresses such matters as tax incidence (who really pays a particular tax), cost–benefit
analysis of government programmes, effects on economic efficiency and income distribution of different kinds of
spending and taxes, and fiscal politics. The latter, an aspect of public choice theory, models public-sector behaviour in
ways analogous to those in microeconomics, involving interactions among self-interested voters, politicians, and
bureaucrats.
Much of economics is positive, seeking to describe and predict economic phenomena. Normative economics seeks to
identify what economies ought to be like.
Welfare economics is a normative branch of economics that uses <color=#3366CC>microeconomic</color> techniques to simultaneously
determine the <color=#3366CC>allocative efficiency</color> within an economy and the income <color=#3366CC>distribution</color> associated with it. It attempts to
measure <color=#3366CC>social welfare</color> by examining the economic activities of the individuals that comprise society.
International economics
International trade studies the determinants of the flows of goods and services across international boundaries. It also
concerns the size and distribution of gains from trade. Policy applications include estimating the effects of changing
<color=#3366CC>tariff</color> rates and trade quotas. International finance is a macroeconomic field that examines the flow of capital across
international borders and the effects of these movements on <color=#3366CC>exchange rates</color>. Increased trade in goods, services, and
capital between countries is a major effect of contemporary <color=#3366CC>globalisation</color>.
Labour economics
Labour economics seeks to understand the functioning and dynamics of the <color=#3366CC>markets</color> for wage labour. Labour markets
function through the interaction of workers and employers. Labour economics examines the supply of labour services
(workers), the demand for labour services (employers), and the resulting patterns of wages, employment, and income.
In economics, labour is a measure of the work done by human beings. It is conventionally contrasted with such other
<color=#3366CC>factors of production</color> as land and <color=#3366CC>capital</color>.
Development economics
Development economics examines economic aspects of the economic development process in relatively <color=#3366CC>low-income</color>
<color=#3366CC>countries</color>, focusing on structural change, <color=#3366CC>poverty</color>, and <color=#3366CC>economic growth</color>. Approaches in development economics
frequently incorporate social and political factors.
Related subjects
Economics is one of several <color=#3366CC>social sciences</color>. It has fields bordering on other areas, including <color=#3366CC>economic geography</color>,
<color=#3366CC>economic history</color>, public choice, energy economics, cultural economics, family economics and institutional economics.
Law and economics, or economic analysis of law, is an approach to legal theory that applies economic methods to law.
It includes the use of economic concepts to explain the effects of legal rules, to assess which legal rules are
economically efficient, and to predict what the legal rules will be. A seminal article by <color=#3366CC>Ronald Coase</color> published in 1961
suggested that well-defined property rights could overcome the problems of <color=#3366CC>externalities</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Political economy</color> is the interdisciplinary study that combines economics, law, and <color=#3366CC>political science</color> to explain how
political institutions, the political environment, and the economic system (capitalist, <color=#3366CC>socialist</color>, mixed) influence one
another. It studies questions such as how monopoly, rent-seeking behaviour, and <color=#3366CC>externalities</color> should impact
government policy. <color=#3366CC>Historians</color> have employed political economy to explore the ways in the past that persons and
groups with common economic interests have used politics to effect changes beneficial to their interests.
Energy economics is a broad <color=#3366CC>scientific</color> subject area which includes topics related to energy supply and energy demand.
<color=#3366CC>Georgescu-Roegen</color> reintroduced the concept of <color=#3366CC>entropy</color> in economics and energy, drawing on <color=#3366CC>thermodynamics</color>, as
opposed to what he viewed as the mechanistic foundation of neoclassical economics, rooted in Newtonian physics. His
work contributed significantly to thermoeconomics and to ecological economics. He also did foundational work, which
later developed into evolutionary economics.
The <color=#3366CC>sociological</color> subfield of economic sociology arose, primarily through the work of <color=#3366CC>Émile Durkheim</color>, <color=#3366CC>Max Weber</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Georg Simmel</color>, as an approach to analysing the effects of economic phenomena in relation to the overarching social
paradigm (i.e., <color=#3366CC>modernity</color>). Classic works include Max Weber's <color=#3366CC>The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism</color> (1905)
and Georg Simmel's The Philosophy of Money (1900). More recently, the works of <color=#3366CC>James S. Coleman</color>, Mark
Granovetter, Peter Hedstrom and Richard Swedberg have been influential in this field.
<color=#3366CC>Gary Becker</color> in 1974 presented an economic theory of social interactions, whose applications included the family,
charity, merit goods, and multiperson interactions, and envy and hatred. He and Kevin Murphy authored a book in 2001
that analysed market behaviour in a social environment.
Profession
The professionalisation of economics, reflected in the growth of graduate programmes on the subject, has been
described as "the main change in economics since around 1900". Most major <color=#3366CC>universities</color> and many colleges have a
major, school, or department in which <color=#3366CC>academic degrees</color> are awarded in the subject, whether in the <color=#3366CC>liberal arts</color>,
business, or for professional study. See Bachelor of Economics and Master of Economics.
In the private sector, professional economists are employed as consultants and in industry, including <color=#3366CC>banking</color> and
<color=#3366CC>finance</color>. Economists also work for various government departments and agencies, for example, the national treasury,
<color=#3366CC>central bank</color>, or National Bureau of Statistics.
There are dozens of prizes awarded to economists each year for outstanding intellectual contributions to the field, the
most prominent of which is the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. However, it is not a <color=#3366CC>Nobel Prize</color>.

Contemporary economics uses mathematics. Economists draw on the tools of <color=#3366CC>calculus</color>, <color=#3366CC>linear algebra</color>, <color=#3366CC>statistics</color>, <color=#3366CC>game</color>
<color=#3366CC>theory</color>, and <color=#3366CC>computer science</color>. Professional economists are expected to be familiar with these tools, while a minority
specialise in econometrics and mathematical methods.
Women in economics
<color=#3366CC>Harriet Martineau</color> (1802–1876) was a widely-read populariser of classical economic thought. Mary Paley Marshall
(1850–1944), the first woman lecturer at a British economics faculty, wrote The Economics of Industry with her
husband <color=#3366CC>Alfred Marshall</color>. <color=#3366CC>Joan Robinson</color> (1903–1983) was an important post-Keynesian economist. The economic
historian Anna Schwartz (1915–2012) coauthored A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960 with <color=#3366CC>Milton</color>
<color=#3366CC>Friedman</color>. Three women have received the Nobel Prize in Economics: <color=#3366CC>Elinor Ostrom</color> (2009), <color=#3366CC>Esther Duflo</color> (2019) and
Claudia Goldin (2023). Five have received the John Bates Clark Medal: Susan Athey (2007), Esther Duflo (2010), Amy
Finkelstein (2012), Emi Nakamura (2019), and Melissa Dell (2020).
Women's authorship share in prominent economic journals reduced from 1940 to the 1970s, but has subsequently
risen, with different patterns of gendered coauthorship. Women remain globally under-represented in the profession
(19% of authors in the RePEc database in 2018), with national variation.
Penn & Teller
Penn & Teller (Penn Jillette and Teller) are American magicians, entertainers, and <color=#3366CC>scientific skeptics</color> who have
performed together since 1975. They are noted for their ongoing act that combines elements of <color=#3366CC>comedy</color> with <color=#3366CC>magic</color>.
The duo has been featured in numerous stage and television shows such as Penn & Teller: Fool Us and currently
perform in Las Vegas at The Rio, the longest-running headliners to play at the same hotel in Las Vegas history. Jillette
serves as the act's <color=#3366CC>orator</color> and raconteur. Teller generally does not speak while performing, but communicates through
<color=#3366CC>mime</color> and <color=#3366CC>nonverbals</color>, though his voice can occasionally be heard during their live shows and television appearances.
Besides magic, the pair has become associated with the advocacy of <color=#3366CC>scientific skepticism</color> and <color=#3366CC>libertarianism</color>,
particularly through their television show Penn & Teller: Bullshit!
Career
Penn and Teller were introduced to each other by Weir Chrisemer, and they performed their first show together at the
Minnesota Renaissance Festival on August 19, 1975. From the late 1970s through 1981, Penn, Teller, and Chrisemer
performed as a trio called "The Asparagus Valley Cultural Society", which played in Philadelphia’s Walnut Street
Theater, and in <color=#3366CC>San Francisco</color>, California, at the Phoenix Theater. Chrisemer helped to develop some bits that
continued, most notably Teller's "Shadows" trick, which involves a single red rose. The group disbanded in 1981 after
Chrisemer quit show business, leaving Penn Jillette and Teller to work as a pair on a show called "Mrs. Lonsberry's
Seance of Horror".
By 1985, Penn & Teller were receiving positive reviews for their Off Broadway show and <color=#3366CC>Emmy Award</color>–winning <color=#3366CC>PBS</color>
special Penn & Teller Go Public. In 1987, they began the first of three <color=#3366CC>Broadway</color> runs. The same year, they appeared
as three-card Monte <color=#3366CC>scam artists</color> in the <color=#3366CC>music video</color> for "It's Tricky" by <color=#3366CC>Run-DMC</color>. Through the late 1980s and early
1990s, the duo made numerous television appearances on Late Night with David Letterman and <color=#3366CC>Saturday Night Live</color>,
as well as The Tonight Show with Jay Leno, Late Night with Conan O'Brien, <color=#3366CC>Today</color>, and others.
Penn & Teller had national tours throughout the 1990s, gaining critical praise. They have also made television guest
appearances on <color=#3366CC>Babylon 5</color> (as the comedy team Rebo and Zooty), The Drew Carey Show, a few episodes of
Hollywood Squares from 1998 until 2004, ABC's Muppets Tonight, FOX's The Bernie Mac Show, an episode of the
game show Fear Factor on NBC, NBC's <color=#3366CC>The West Wing</color>, in a two-part episode of the final season of ABC's Home
Improvement in 1998, four episodes during season 1 of Sabrina, the Teenage Witch in 1996, NBC's Las Vegas, and
Fox's <color=#3366CC>The Simpsons</color> episodes "Hello Gutter, Hello Fadder" and "The Great Simpsina" and the <color=#3366CC>Futurama</color> film Futurama:
Into the Wild Green Yonder in 2009. They appeared in the music video for <color=#3366CC>Katy Perry</color>'s 2009 single "Waking Up in
Vegas", in which they are thrown out of a hotel room by Perry.
Penn and Teller made an appearance on Bill Nye the Science Guy season 2, episode 7 - "Light Optics".
From 2003 to 2010, their Showtime television show Bullshit! took a <color=#3366CC>skeptical</color> look at psychics, <color=#3366CC>religion</color>, the
<color=#3366CC>pseudoscientific</color>, conspiracy theories, and the paranormal. It has featured critical segments on gun control, <color=#3366CC>astrology</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Feng Shui</color>, <color=#3366CC>environmental issues</color>, <color=#3366CC>PETA</color>, <color=#3366CC>weight loss</color>, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the <color=#3366CC>war on drugs</color>.
The pair have written several books about magic, including Penn & Teller's Cruel Tricks For Dear Friends, Penn &
Teller's How to Play with Your Food, and Penn & Teller's How to Play in Traffic. Since 2001, Penn & Teller have
performed in Las Vegas at the Rio All Suite Hotel and Casino.
Penn Jillette hosted a weekday one-hour talk show on Infinity Broadcasting's Free FM radio network from January 3,
2006, to March 2, 2007, with cohost Michael Goudeau. He also hosted the game show Identity, which debuted on
December 18, 2006, on NBC.
Their television series Penn & Teller Tell a Lie premiered on the <color=#3366CC>Discovery Channel</color> on October 5, 2011.
Since 2010, Penn & Teller have hosted Penn & Teller: Fool Us, originally on <color=#3366CC>ITV</color>, moving to <color=#3366CC>The CW</color> in 2015.
Penn & Teller credit magician and <color=#3366CC>skeptical activist</color> <color=#3366CC>James Randi</color> for their own careers. During an interview at TAM!
2012, Penn stated that Randi's book Flim-Flam! was an early influence on him, and said that "If not for Randi there
would not be Penn & Teller as we are today."
In early 2022, Penn and Teller competed in season seven of The Masked Singer as "Hydra" of Team Bad. Because of
Hydra's three-legged design and large size, the costume had to be assembled back stage while "Hydra" had to be
wheeled out on a special platform to get it to and from the stage. Penn operated the left side of "Hydra" while Teller
operated the right side of "Hydra". They were eliminated on the week of April 6 where it was shown that Teller used a
puppet of a rabbit in a hat to "operate" the central head of "Hydra". Teller was given most of the singing due to how
rarely people hear his voice and the possibility of people recognizing Penn's voice. Nicole Byer, who was the guest
panelist of the night, successfully guessed the duo to be underneath the "Hydra" masks.
Off-stage relationship
Jillette stated in a video where he and Teller responded to questions from members of <color=#3366CC>Reddit</color>, and also in a video
interview for Big Think, that while he and Teller share few interests outside magic, Teller is his best friend, and his
children treat Teller as a close relative. He stated that while most entertainment partnerships such as <color=#3366CC>Martin and Lewis</color>
and Lennon–McCartney were based on a deep affection for each other that lends to a certain volatility when things go
wrong, their business relationship and friendship is based on a respect for each other. Teller has made similar
statements. In an <color=#3366CC>NPR</color> interview, Teller said their disagreements often lead to better artistic decisions because they
bring out new ideas and expand the range of discussion.
Honors
On April 5, 2013, Penn & Teller were honored with the 2,494th star on the <color=#3366CC>Hollywood Walk of Fame</color> for their
achievement in the category of Live Performance. Their star is a few steps away from the star of <color=#3366CC>Harry Houdini</color> and
down the street from The Magic Castle. For years they were denied entry to The Magic Circle due to their tendencies to
reveal how magic tricks are done during performances, but in 2025 they were finally given membership during their
50th-anniversary residency at the London Palladium.
They are also recipients of a Hugh M. Hefner First Amendment Award.
In 2007, they won the Scripps Howard Super Sage Award. Their prediction of Indianapolis beating Chicago, 28-17, in
Super Bowl XLI tied for the closest to the actual final score of 29-17 out of the 100 celebrities who participated in the
Scripps Howard Celebrity Super Bowl Poll. They won a coin flip with <color=#3366CC>Michael Phelps</color> and <color=#3366CC>Buzz Aldrin</color> who made the
same prediction.
In 2014, they were nominated for a BAFTA Award for their documentary Tim's Vermeer.
For their contributions to the <color=#3366CC>West End</color> production Magic Goes Wrong with Mischief Theatre, they were nominated for a
2020 <color=#3366CC>Olivier Award</color>.
Tricks
Penn & Teller perform their own adaptation of the famous bullet catch illusion. Each simultaneously fires a gun at the
other through small panes of glass and then "catches" the other's bullet in his mouth. They also have an assortment of
<color=#3366CC>card tricks</color> in their repertoire, virtually all of them involving the force of the Three of Clubs on an unsuspecting audience
member as this card is easy for viewers to identify on television cameras.
In one of their most politically charged tricks, they make an <color=#3366CC>American flag</color> seem to disappear by wrapping it in a copy of
the <color=#3366CC>United States Bill of Rights</color>, and apparently setting the flag on fire, so that "the flag is gone but the Bill of Rights
remains". The routine may also feature the "Chinese bill of rights", presented as a transparent piece of acetate. They
normally end the trick by restoring the unscathed flag to its starting place on the flagpole; however, on a TV guest
appearance on <color=#3366CC>The West Wing</color>, this final part was omitted. The methods of the trick were revealed by the duo in an
episode of Fool Us. In 2025 <color=#3366CC>the New York Times</color> reported that the duo had stopped performing this trick because of the
association between the American flag and the Make America Great Again movement.
One trick involves a powered <color=#3366CC>nail gun</color> with a quantity of missing nails from the series of nails in its <color=#3366CC>magazine</color>. Penn
begins by firing several apparently real nails into a board in front of him. He then proceeds to fire the nail gun into the
palm of his hand several times, while suffering no injuries. His pattern builds as he oscillates between firing blanks into
his hand and firing nails into the board, and fires one blank into Teller's crotch. Near the end of the trick, he says that it
is a trick and that he and Teller believe that it is morally wrong to do things on stage that are really dangerous—it
makes the audience complicit in unnecessary human risk.
A trick introduced in 2010 is a modern version of the bag escape, replacing the traditional sack with a black trash bag
apparently filled with <color=#3366CC>helium</color>. Teller is placed in the bag which is then pumped full of helium and sealed by an audience
member. For the escape, the audience is blinded by a bright light for a second and when they are able to see again,
Teller has escaped from the bag and Penn is holding it, still full of helium, above his head, before releasing it to float to
the ceiling. The duo had hoped to put the trick in their mini-tour in London; however, it was first shown to the public in
their Las Vegas show on August 18, 2010. In June 2011, Penn & Teller performed this trick for the first time in the
United Kingdom on their <color=#3366CC>ITV</color> show Fool Us.
In one of their TV appearances on The Tonight Show, they performed a trick that involved all members of the audience.
Each person received four cards which were torn apart and "mixed" so as to have two out of the eight halves selected
in a process that seems random, as each person has freedom of moves throughout the process. Yet in the end,
everyone ends up with two halves of the same card. Some mathematicians made a deep analysis of the trick and
generalized it so it would work with any number of initial cards, using <color=#3366CC>mathematical induction</color>; their complete analysis
was published in the Journal of Magic Research.
Politics and personal lives
On Bullshit!, the duo described their social and political views as libertarian. In addition to disbelief in the <color=#3366CC>paranormal</color>
and <color=#3366CC>pseudoscience</color>, Penn & Teller also take a view of doubtfulness to government authority. In various episodes of
their show, they have heavily criticized both the Internal Revenue Service and the <color=#3366CC>Environmental Protection Agency</color>, as
well as taken stances against <color=#3366CC>circumcision</color> and gun control, and in support of ideas such as freedom to eat fast food,
private property, and lower taxes. Penn & Teller were both <color=#3366CC>H. L. Mencken</color> research fellows with the Cato Institute, a
libertarian think-tank and research organization. Penn disavowed libertarianism in 2020, though is still affiliated with the
Cato Institute.
Penn & Teller have shown support for the Brights movement and are now listed on the movement's website under the
Enthusiastic Brights section.
They have described themselves as teetotalers.
In March 2026 they filed a friend of the court brief asking the <color=#3366CC>United States Supreme Court</color> to hear the appeal of a
convicted murderer. The witness who identified the defendant had undergone hypnosis by the detective investigating
the case. Penn told <color=#3366CC>the New York Times</color> "I think the evidence is bogus" and “the way they got the evidence was about
the level of seriousness of a Las Vegas goofball magician.”

The 1995 video game Penn & Teller's Smoke and Mirrors featured a mini-game called Desert Bus in which the player
drove a bus route between Tucson and Las Vegas. Once reaching the destination, the player gets one point and, if
desired, can then drive the return route. The game was considered by some to be long and boring yet found a cult
audience. The entire set of games was actually more of a collection of tricks and pranks, rather than games meant to
be actually good to play. Both in-game and in interviews Penn states that Desert Bus was a reaction to the controversy
of violent video-games going on at the time. In essence making fun of this controversy, by creating a simulator
"stupefyingly like reality".
The game has since been used in an annual charity event called "Desert Bus for Hope" run by the Canadian internet
comedy troupe LoadingReadyRun. The fundraiser involves members of LoadingReadyRun (and occasional guests)
playing the game and streaming that live online, while interviewing celebrities via Skype and accepting challenges for
the audience, with all proceeds being donated to Child's Play. On November 14, 2011, an <color=#3366CC>iOS</color> port of Desert Bus was
created and released in the iTunes Store. The game was developed in conjunction with the Desert Bus For Hope event
and all profits from the game are donated to charity.
